concept.concept_description: Prove that the Birkhoff polytope B_n has the clique-face property if and only if n ≤ 3. For n=3, explicitly characterize all cliques in the 1-skeleton and verify they correspond to faces. For n=4, construct a specific 4-clique in the 1-skeleton that is not the vertex set of any face, using the fact that two permutation matrices are adjacent in B_n iff the corresponding permutations differ by a single transposition. Formalize the 1-skeleton as a graph on S_n with edges given by transpositions, define the clique-face property precisely, and prove the dichotomy.
concept.mathematical_framing: Let B_n be the Birkhoff polytope, the convex hull in R^(n x n) of all n x n permutation matrices. Conjecture: B_n satisfies the clique-face property, meaning every clique in the 1-skeleton of B_n is exactly the vertex set of a face, if and only if n <= 2.
concept.lean_guess: For n <= 2, B_n is respectively a point or a segment, so the clique-face property is immediate. For n = 3, two permutation vertices are adjacent exactly when their quotient permutation has a single nontrivial cycle; every nonidentity element of S_3 has this property, so the 1-skeleton of B_3 is complete on six vertices. However B_3 is 4-dimensional and its facets are given by equations x_ij = 0, each containing only four permutation vertices, so a five-vertex clique is not the vertex set of any face. Thus B_3 fails the property. For n >= 3, B_n contains a face isomorphic to B_3 by fixing n-3 rows and columns to the corresponding identity entries. Since the clique-face property passes to faces, B_n also fails it.

import Mathlib

/-!
# The clique–face question for the Birkhoff polytope `B₃`

The **Birkhoff polytope** `Bₙ` is the polytope of `n × n` doubly stochastic
matrices; by the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem it is the convex hull of the `n!`
permutation matrices, which are exactly its vertices.

Its **graph** (`1`-skeleton) has the permutation matrices as vertices, two of
them being *adjacent* when the segment joining them is an edge (a `1`-dimensional
face) of the polytope.  A **clique** of this graph is a set of pairwise-adjacent
vertices.

A natural guess — call it the *clique–face conjecture* — is that every clique is
the vertex set of a face, i.e. that for a clique `K` the convex hull
`convexHull ℝ K` is a face of `Bₙ`.

This file **disproves** the clique–face conjecture for `n = 3`.  In `B₃` *every*
pair of distinct vertices is adjacent (the graph is the complete graph `K₆`), so
in particular the three even permutations

```
A₃ = { id , (0 1 2) , (0 2 1) }
```

form a clique.  But their convex hull is **not** a face of `B₃`: its centroid is
the barycenter `(1/3)·J` of the whole polytope, which also lies in the interior
of segments leaving the triangle.  Hence the clique–face conjecture fails.

## Main results

* `matI`, `matC1`, `matC2`, `matT01`, `matT02`, `matT12` — the six vertices.
* `edge_I_C1`, `edge_I_C2`, `edge_C1_C2` — the three edges of the triangle `A₃`
  are genuine faces (`IsExtreme`) of `B₃`; so `A₃` is a clique.
* `not_face_A3` — `convexHull ℝ {matI, matC1, matC2}` is **not** a face of `B₃`.
* `cliqueFaceConjecture_false` — the clique–face conjecture is false for `B₃`.

All faces are taken in the sense of `IsExtreme ℝ B₃`.
-/

noncomputable section

open Matrix Finset

namespace BirkhoffCliqueFace

/-- The ambient space of `3 × 3` real matrices. -/
abbrev M := Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℝ

/-- The Birkhoff polytope `B₃` as a set of matrices. -/
def B3 : Set M := (doublyStochastic ℝ (Fin 3) : Set M)

theorem mem_B3 {X : M} :
    X ∈ B3 ↔ (∀ i j, 0 ≤ X i j) ∧ (∀ i, ∑ j, X i j = 1) ∧ (∀ j, ∑ i, X i j = 1) :=
  mem_doublyStochastic_iff_sum

theorem convex_B3 : Convex ℝ B3 := convex_doublyStochastic

/-! ### The six vertices (permutation matrices) -/

/-- identity -/
def matI : M := !![1, 0, 0; 0, 1, 0; 0, 0, 1]
/-- the `3`-cycle `(0 1 2)` -/
def matC1 : M := !![0, 1, 0; 0, 0, 1; 1, 0, 0]
/-- the `3`-cycle `(0 2 1)` -/
def matC2 : M := !![0, 0, 1; 1, 0, 0; 0, 1, 0]
/-- the transposition `(0 1)` -/
def matT01 : M := !![0, 1, 0; 1, 0, 0; 0, 0, 1]
/-- the transposition `(0 2)` -/
def matT02 : M := !![0, 0, 1; 0, 1, 0; 1, 0, 0]
/-- the transposition `(1 2)` -/
def matT12 : M := !![1, 0, 0; 0, 0, 1; 0, 1, 0]

/-- The set of vertices of `B₃`: the permutation matrices. -/
def vertices : Set M := {X | ∃ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin 3), σ.permMatrix ℝ = X}

theorem matI_mem_B3 : matI ∈ B3 := by
  constructor;
  · norm_num [ Fin.forall_fin_succ, matI ];
  · constructor <;> ext i <;> fin_cases i <;> norm_num [ matI ];
    all_goals rfl;

theorem matC1_mem_B3 : matC1 ∈ B3 := by
  constructor;
  · norm_num [ Fin.forall_fin_succ, matC1 ];
  · simp +decide [ matC1, ← List.ofFn_inj ];
    simp +decide [ vecHead, vecTail ]

theorem matC2_mem_B3 : matC2 ∈ B3 := by
  constructor;
  · norm_num [ Fin.forall_fin_succ, matC2 ];
  · simp +decide [ matC2, ← List.ofFn_inj ];
    simp +decide [ vecHead, vecTail ]

theorem matT01_mem_B3 : matT01 ∈ B3 := by
  constructor;
  · norm_num [ Fin.forall_fin_succ, matT01 ];
  · simp +decide [ matT01, funext_iff, Fin.forall_fin_succ ];
    exact ⟨ rfl, rfl, rfl ⟩

theorem matT02_mem_B3 : matT02 ∈ B3 := by
  simp [matT02, mem_B3, Fin.sum_univ_three];
  norm_num [ Fin.forall_fin_succ ]

theorem matT12_mem_B3 : matT12 ∈ B3 := by
  constructor;
  · norm_num [ Fin.forall_fin_succ, matT12 ];
  · norm_num [ ← List.ofFn_inj, matT12 ];
    exact ⟨ rfl, rfl, rfl ⟩

theorem matI_mem_vertices : matI ∈ vertices := by
  use 1; simp +decide [Equiv.Perm.permMatrix];
  exact Matrix.ext fun i j => by fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> rfl;

theorem matC1_mem_vertices : matC1 ∈ vertices := by
  use finRotate 3;
  ext i j; fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> simp +decide [ Equiv.Perm.permMatrix ] ;
  all_goals rfl;

theorem matC2_mem_vertices : matC2 ∈ vertices := by
  use (finRotate 3)^2;
  ext i j ; fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> simp +decide [ Equiv.Perm.permMatrix ];
  all_goals rfl;

/-! ### Faces and adjacency -/

/-- A *face* of `B₃` is an extreme subset. -/
def IsFace (F : Set M) : Prop := IsExtreme ℝ B3 F

/-- A *clique* is a set of vertices that are pairwise adjacent, i.e. every pair
spans a face (an edge) of `B₃`. -/
def IsClique (K : Set M) : Prop :=
  K ⊆ vertices ∧ ∀ a ∈ K, ∀ b ∈ K, a ≠ b → IsFace (segment ℝ a b)

/-- The *clique–face conjecture* for `B₃`: every clique is the vertex set of a
face, i.e. its convex hull is a face. -/
def CliqueFaceConjecture : Prop :=
  ∀ K : Set M, IsClique K → IsFace (convexHull ℝ K)

/-! ### A reusable "zero-pattern face" criterion

If a subset `S ⊆ B₃` is exactly the set of doubly stochastic matrices that
vanish on a fixed list of cells, then `S` is a face.  This is because vanishing
on a cell is preserved under taking endpoints of an open segment (all entries
are nonnegative). -/

theorem face_of_zeros (S : Set M) (cells : List (Fin 3 × Fin 3))
    (hSsub : S ⊆ B3)
    (hSzero : ∀ X ∈ S, ∀ c ∈ cells, X c.1 c.2 = 0)
    (hzeroS : ∀ X ∈ B3, (∀ c ∈ cells, X c.1 c.2 = 0) → X ∈ S) :
    IsFace S := by
      refine' ⟨ hSsub, _ ⟩;
      intros x hx y hy z hz hzy
      obtain ⟨a, b, ha, hb, hab, hz_eq⟩ : ∃ a b : ℝ, 0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧ a + b = 1 ∧ a • x + b • y = z := by
        rcases hzy with ⟨ a, b, ha, hb, hab, rfl ⟩ ; exact ⟨ a, b, ha, hb, hab, rfl ⟩ ;
      refine' hzeroS x hx _;
      intros c hc
      have hz_zero : z c.1 c.2 = 0 := by
        exact hSzero z hz c hc;
      have h_nonneg : 0 ≤ x c.1 c.2 ∧ 0 ≤ y c.1 c.2 := by
        exact ⟨ mem_B3.mp hx |>.1 _ _, mem_B3.mp hy |>.1 _ _ ⟩;
      replace hz_eq := congr_fun ( congr_fun hz_eq c.1 ) c.2; norm_num at hz_eq; nlinarith;

/-! ### The three edges of the triangle `A₃` are faces -/

/-
The edge between `id` and `(0 1 2)` is a face: it is cut out by forcing the
support of `(0 2 1)` (the cells `(0,2), (1,0), (2,1)`) to be zero.
-/
theorem edge_I_C1 : IsFace (segment ℝ matI matC1) := by
  apply face_of_zeros;
  case cells => exact [ ( 0, 2 ), ( 1, 0 ), ( 2, 1 ) ];
  · exact convex_B3.segment_subset matI_mem_B3 matC1_mem_B3;
  · simp +decide [ segment_eq_image ];
    rintro X x hx₁ hx₂ rfl; simp +decide [ matI, matC1 ] ;
  · intro X hX hzeroS
    have h_eq : X 1 1 = X 0 0 ∧ X 1 2 = X 0 1 ∧ X 2 0 = X 0 1 ∧ X 2 2 = X 0 0 := by
      simp_all +decide [ Fin.sum_univ_three, mem_B3 ];
      grind;
    simp_all +decide [ segment_eq_image, mem_B3 ];
    use X 0 1;
    simp_all +decide [ Fin.forall_fin_succ, Fin.sum_univ_three ];
    exact ⟨ by linarith, by ext i j; fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> simp +decide [ *, matI, matC1 ] <;> linarith ⟩

/-
The edge between `id` and `(0 2 1)` is a face.
-/
theorem edge_I_C2 : IsFace (segment ℝ matI matC2) := by
  convert face_of_zeros ( segment ℝ matI matC2 ) [ ( 0, 1 ), ( 1, 2 ), ( 2, 0 ) ] _ _ _ using 1;
  · exact convex_B3.segment_subset ( matI_mem_B3 ) ( matC2_mem_B3 );
  · simp +decide [ segment_eq_image, matI, matC2 ];
    aesop;
  · intro X hX h_zero
    obtain ⟨a, b, ha, hb, hab, hX_eq⟩ : ∃ a b : ℝ, 0 ≤ a ∧ 0 ≤ b ∧ a + b = 1 ∧ X = a • matI + b • matC2 := by
      simp_all +decide [ mem_B3 ];
      simp_all +decide [ Fin.forall_fin_succ, Fin.sum_univ_succ ];
      use X 0 0, by linarith, X 0 2, by linarith, by linarith, by ext i j; fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> simp +decide [ *, matI, matC2 ] <;> linarith!;
    exact hX_eq.symm ▸ ⟨ a, b, ha, hb, hab, rfl ⟩

/-
The edge between `(0 1 2)` and `(0 2 1)` is a face.
-/
theorem edge_C1_C2 : IsFace (segment ℝ matC1 matC2) := by
  -- Apply the face_of_zeros theorem with the cells (0,0), (1,1), and (2,2).
  apply face_of_zeros (segment ℝ matC1 matC2) [(0,0), (1,1), (2,2)];
  · exact convex_B3.segment_subset matC1_mem_B3 matC2_mem_B3;
  · simp +decide [ segment_eq_image ];
    rintro X x hx₁ hx₂ rfl; simp +decide [ matC1, matC2 ] ;
  · simp +decide [ mem_B3 ];
    intro X hX₁ hX₂ hX₃ hX₄ hX₅ hX₆; simp_all +decide [ Fin.forall_fin_succ, Fin.sum_univ_succ ] ;
    unfold matC1 matC2; simp +decide [ segment_eq_image ] ;
    exact ⟨ X 0 2, ⟨ by linarith, by linarith ⟩, by ext i j; fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> norm_num <;> linarith! ⟩

/-
The three even permutations form a clique in the graph of `B₃`.
-/
theorem A3_isClique : IsClique {matI, matC1, matC2} := by
  constructor;
  · rintro X ( rfl | rfl | rfl ) <;> [ exact matI_mem_vertices; exact matC1_mem_vertices; exact matC2_mem_vertices ];
  · simp [edge_I_C1, edge_I_C2, edge_C1_C2];
    exact ⟨ fun _ => by simpa only [ segment_symm ] using edge_I_C1, fun _ => by simpa only [ segment_symm ] using edge_I_C2, fun _ => by simpa only [ segment_symm ] using edge_C1_C2 ⟩

/-! ### The triangle `A₃` is not a face -/

/-
The triangle `convexHull ℝ {id, (012), (021)}` is **not** a face of `B₃`.
-/
theorem not_face_A3 : ¬ IsFace (convexHull ℝ {matI, matC1, matC2}) := by
  rintro ⟨ h1, h2 ⟩;
  contrapose! h2;
  refine' ⟨ matT01, _, ( 1 / 2 : ℝ ) • matT02 + ( 1 / 2 : ℝ ) • matT12, _, _ ⟩ <;> norm_num [ openSegment_eq_image ];
  · grind +suggestions;
  · convert convex_B3 matT02_mem_B3 matT12_mem_B3 ( by norm_num : ( 0 : ℝ ) ≤ 1 / 2 ) ( by norm_num : ( 0 : ℝ ) ≤ 1 / 2 ) ( by norm_num ) using 1;
  · refine' ⟨ _, _, ⟨ 2 / 3, _, rfl ⟩, _ ⟩ <;> norm_num;
    · refine' mem_convexHull_iff.mpr _;
      intro t ht ht'; have := ht ( Set.mem_insert _ _ ) ; have := ht ( Set.mem_insert_of_mem _ ( Set.mem_insert _ _ ) ) ; have := ht ( Set.mem_insert_of_mem _ ( Set.mem_insert_of_mem _ ( Set.mem_singleton _ ) ) ) ; norm_num at * ;
      convert ht' ‹matI ∈ t› ( ht' ‹matC1 ∈ t› ‹matC2 ∈ t› ( by norm_num : ( 0 : ℝ ) ≤ 1 / 2 ) ( by norm_num : ( 0 : ℝ ) ≤ 1 / 2 ) ( by norm_num ) ) ( by norm_num : ( 0 : ℝ ) ≤ 1 / 3 ) ( by norm_num : ( 0 : ℝ ) ≤ 2 / 3 ) ( by norm_num ) using 1 ; ext i j ; fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> norm_num [ matI, matC1, matC2, matT01, matT02, matT12 ];
    · rw [ convexHull_insert ] <;> norm_num [ matI, matC1, matC2, matT01 ];
      norm_num [ segment_eq_image ];
      rintro x y hy₁ hy₂ rfl z hz₁ hz₂; intro H; have := congr_fun ( congr_fun H 0 ) 1; norm_num at this; have := congr_fun ( congr_fun H 1 ) 0; norm_num at this; have := congr_fun ( congr_fun H 2 ) 0; norm_num at this; linarith;

/-! ### The clique–face conjecture is false for `B₃` -/

/-- **Counterexample (n = 3).**  The clique–face conjecture fails for the
Birkhoff polytope `B₃`: the clique `A₃` is not the vertex set of any face. -/
theorem cliqueFaceConjecture_false : ¬ CliqueFaceConjecture := by
  intro h
  exact not_face_A3 (h {matI, matC1, matC2} A3_isClique)

end BirkhoffCliqueFace

# Computational Evidence: clique-face property of Birkhoff polytopes

We test the conjecture **"`B_n` satisfies the clique-face property iff `n ≤ 2`"** in the
combinatorial model used in `Skeleton.lean` / `CliqueFace.lean`.

Recall the model:
* Vertices of `B_n` = permutations of `Fin n` (there are `n!` of them; these are the extreme
  points of the doubly stochastic matrices, Mathlib `extremePoints_doublyStochastic`).
* 1-skeleton (Brualdi–Gibson): `σ ~ τ` iff `σ⁻¹ τ` is a single cycle.
* Face vertex sets (Billera–Sarangarajan): `S` is a face vertex set iff every permutation
  whose graph lies in the union of the graphs of `S` already belongs to `S`.

## 1. Small cases

### n = 1
* 1 vertex (`id`). Skeleton: no edges. Cliques: `∅, {id}`.
* `cellUnion {id} = {(0,0)}`; the only permutation supported there is `id`. Both cliques are
  face vertex sets. **Property holds.**

### n = 2
* 2 vertices: `id`, `(0 1)`. Their graphs `{(0,0),(1,1)}` and `{(0,1),(1,0)}` are **disjoint**.
* Skeleton = `K_2` (one edge, since `(0 1)` is a single cycle).
* Every subset is a face vertex set, because disjoint graphs force any permutation supported
  on `cellUnion S` to coincide with a member of `S`. **Property holds.**

### n = 3
* 6 vertices. Every non-identity element of `S_3` is a transposition or a 3-cycle — all single
  cycles — so the skeleton is the **complete graph `K_6`**: every subset is a clique.
* Counterexample clique: the three transpositions `(0 1), (0 2), (1 2)`.
  * support union (`cellUnion`):
    | from\to | 0 | 1 | 2 |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | 0 | • | • | • |
    | 1 | • | • | • |
    | 2 | • | • | • |

    All 9 cells are occupied (each diagonal cell `(i,i)` is fixed by one of the transpositions;
    each off-diagonal cell is realised by the transposition swapping those coordinates).
  * Hence **every** permutation of `Fin 3` is supported on the union; in particular the 3-cycle
    `(0 1 2)` is supported there but is **not** one of the three transpositions.
  * So this size-3 clique is not a face vertex set (its smallest enclosing face is the whole
    polytope, with all 6 vertices). **Property fails.**

## 2. The structural phase transition

Distinct permutations of `Fin n` have pairwise-disjoint graphs **iff** `n ≤ 2`:
* `n ≤ 2`: a permutation of a ≤2-element set fixing one point is the identity, so distinct
  permutations disagree everywhere (verified by `decide` in `disjointGraphs_fin`).
* `n ≥ 3`: the transpositions `(0 1)` and `(0 2)` both fix every coordinate `≥ 3` and agree
  there (e.g. both fix `1`? no — but both fix coordinate `j ≥ 3`), so their graphs share cells.
  More simply, `(0 1)` and `id` agree at coordinate `2`.

This disjointness is precisely what makes "support closure" collapse to "membership", which is
why the clique-face property is equivalent to `n ≤ 2`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt for `n ≥ 3`

The three-transposition clique generalises verbatim to every `n ≥ 3`: with points `0,1,2`,
the transpositions `(0 1),(0 2),(1 2)` (fixing all coordinates `≥ 3`) are pairwise adjacent
(their products are 3-cycles), their support union contains the 3-cycle `(0 1 2)`, and that
3-cycle is not among them. This is formalised as `not_cliqueFace_fin_of_three`.

## 4. Conclusion

Computation matches the conjecture exactly: the property holds for `n ∈ {1,2}` and fails for
every `n ≥ 3`. This is fully proved (0 `sorry`, axioms `propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound`)
as `birkhoff_cliqueFace_iff`.

Derived from this cycle's findings (proved: `birkhoff_cliqueFace_iff` — `B_n` has the
clique-face property iff `n ≤ 2`; the mechanism is the disjoint-graph dichotomy and the
three-transposition counterexample for `n ≥ 3`).

For `n ≥ 3`, count the cliques of the 1-skeleton that are **not** face vertex sets, as a
function of `n`. Conjecture: this count grows super-exponentially and admits a clean formula in
terms of subsets of permutations whose support union strictly contains them.
*The key insight is...* a clique fails to be a face exactly when its support union admits a
permutation outside the clique, so "bad cliques" are counted by support patterns with extra
perfect matchings.
*Why now?* We have a verified combinatorial characterisation (`IsFaceVertexSet` via support
closure) that turns the geometric question into a finite enumeration amenable to `decide`.

## Conjecture 2 — Minimal bad clique size
For `n ≥ 3`, the smallest clique that is not a face vertex set has size exactly `3`, realised by
three transpositions, and never smaller.
*The key insight is...* size-2 cliques are edges, and edges are always faces of the Birkhoff
polytope (Brualdi–Gibson), so the first obstruction can only appear at size `3`.
*Why now?* `not_cliqueFace_fin_of_three` already exhibits a size-3 witness; proving minimality
needs only that all 2-element cliques satisfy `IsFaceVertexSet`, a finite local check.

Replace `B_n` by the transportation polytope of nonnegative matrices with prescribed row/column
sums `(r, c)`. Conjecture: the clique-face property holds iff the bipartite support graph forced
by `(r, c)` has no induced structure realising three pairwise-adjacent vertices with full
support — generalising the `n ≤ 2` threshold.
*The key insight is...* the disjoint-graph dichotomy is really a statement about when distinct
vertices can share a support cell, which is governed by the margins `(r, c)`.
*Why now?* Mathlib's `doublyStochastic` development gives the `r = c = 1` case; the support-union
face model ports directly to general margins.

is a complete multipartite graph, and the clique-face failures are exactly its non-maximal
cliques.

makes single-cycle differences ubiquitous, pushing the skeleton toward completeness (already
`K_6` for `n = 3`).
*Why now?* We proved the `n = 3` skeleton is complete; the multipartite refinement is the
natural next falsifiable step with the same `Equiv.Perm.IsCycle` toolkit.

Quotient `B_n` by a cyclic symmetry of the index set. Conjecture: the clique-face threshold

under group actions encoded with `Equiv.Perm` conjugation already in scope.

/-!
# Finite-Size Fluctuation Theorem: Second-Law Violations are Exponentially Rare

**Catalog category (v19a menu): cross-domain bridge.**
This file bridges *finite probability theory* (a Markov/Chernoff tail bound) with the
*thermodynamic* Landauer / second-law development built in `Logic.JarzynskiLandauer`
and `Physics.LandauerSecondLaw`.

`Physics.LandauerSecondLaw` proved the **average** statement of the second law,
`ΔF ≤ E[W]`, and `Physics.LandauerSaturation` characterised its equality case. Neither
controls the *fluctuations*: a genuinely stochastic erasure has individual realisations
whose work `W ω` dips *below* the free-energy bound `ΔF`. The physically sharp
finite-size statement — the integral fluctuation theorem in its Markov-inequality form —
is that such "second-law violations" are **exponentially suppressed**:

> the total probability that the dissipated work is below `ΔF` by a margin `ξ`
> is at most `exp(-α ξ)`,

where `α = (kT)⁻¹` is the inverse temperature. This is a strict refinement of the
average bound: it recovers `ΔF ≤ E[W]` on average yet quantifies the rare events that
locally beat Landauer's limit.

## Main results

* `second_law_violation_bound` — `P(W < ΔF - ξ) ≤ exp(-α ξ)` from the Jarzynski equality.
* `second_law_no_violation_below` — for `ξ ≥ 0` the violation probability is `< 1`
  whenever some outcome lies on/above the bound (the bound cannot be violated with
  certainty).
* `landauer_violation_bound` — specialisation to one-bit erasure: the probability that
  the erasure work falls `ξ` below `k·T·log 2` is at most `exp(-ξ / (kT))`.
* `landauer_violation_decays` — monotone exponential decay of the Landauer violation
  probability bound as the margin `ξ` grows.

## References
- Jarzynski, C. (1997). Nonequilibrium equality for free energy differences.
- Jarzynski, C. (2011). Equalities and inequalities: irreversibility and the second law
  of thermodynamics at the nanoscale.
- Landauer, R. (1961). Irreversibility and heat generation in the computing process.
-/

open BigOperators Real Finset
open JarzynskiLandauer

namespace LandauerFluctuationBound

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): The catalog had only the *average* second law ΔF ≤ E[W] and
--   its equality case. We conjectured a far stronger finite-size statement: the Jarzynski
--   equality forces the *distribution* of work to concentrate above ΔF, so that the
--   probability of a second-law violation of size ξ decays like exp(-αξ). Bold corollary:
--   no genuine erasure can beat Landauer's bound with certainty; violations are exponentially
--   rare in units of kT.
-- Experiment (Experimenter): The key realisation is that E[exp(-αW)] = exp(-αΔF) is exactly
--   a moment generating function identity, so a one-line finite Markov inequality applies.
--   On the violation set S = {W < ΔF - ξ} we have exp(-αW) > exp(-αΔF)·exp(αξ) pointwise;
--   summing p·exp(-αW) over S, bounding below by the constant, and comparing to the full
--   sum exp(-αΔF) (Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg) gives the bound after dividing by
--   the positive constant exp(-αΔF). No measure theory needed — pure finite sums.
-- Analysis (Analyst): This is the integral fluctuation theorem ⟨exp(-α(W-ΔF))⟩ = 1 read as
--   a Chernoff tail bound. The average law ΔF ≤ E[W] is the ξ→ first-moment shadow of this
--   distributional statement; the new content is the exponential SUPPRESSION, the genuinely
--   finite-size / nanoscale correction the mission asks for.
-- Critique (Critic): Need α > 0 (β = 1/kT > 0) to divide by exp(-αΔF) > 0 with the right
--   inequality direction. The filter set needs classical decidability (open Classical). The
--   "< 1" corollary needs a witness outcome at/above the bound with positive probability, else
--   it could be vacuously 1. The proof genuinely uses exp monotonicity + a subset sum bound,
--   not simp/decide.
-- Synthesis (PI): A distributional fluctuation-theorem layer above the average second law,
--   quantifying nanoscale violations of Landauer's bound.
-- !-- end Lab Notes -- !--

open Classical

variable {Ω : Type*} [Fintype Ω]

/-
**Exponential bound on second-law violations (finite Jarzynski / Chernoff).**
Under the finite Jarzynski equality at inverse temperature `α > 0`, the total
probability that the dissipated work `W` falls below the free-energy difference `ΔF`
by a margin `ξ` is at most `exp(-α ξ)`.
-/
theorem second_law_violation_bound (p : Ω → ℝ) (hp : IsPMF p) (W : Ω → ℝ)
    (α ΔF : ℝ) (hα : 0 < α) (hJ : JarzynskiCondition p W α ΔF) (ξ : ℝ) :
    ∑ ω ∈ univ.filter (fun ω => W ω < ΔF - ξ), p ω ≤ Real.exp (-α * ξ) := by
  -- Applying the Jarzynski condition to the set `S = univ.filter (fun ω => W ω < ΔF - ξ)`.
  have h_jarzynski_S : ∑ ω ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun ω => W ω < ΔF - ξ), p ω * Real.exp (-α * W ω) ≤ Real.exp (-α * ΔF) := by
    exact hJ.le.trans' ( Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg ( Finset.filter_subset _ _ ) fun x _ _ => mul_nonneg ( hp.1 _ ) ( Real.exp_nonneg _ ) );
  -- Applying the inequality $p ω * \exp(-α * W ω) ≥ p ω * \exp(-α * (ΔF - ξ))$ for each $ω$ in the set $S$.
  have h_ineq : ∀ ω ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun ω => W ω < ΔF - ξ), p ω * Real.exp (-α * W ω) ≥ p ω * Real.exp (-α * (ΔF - ξ)) := by
    exact fun ω hω => mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( Real.exp_le_exp.mpr ( by nlinarith [ Finset.mem_filter.mp hω ] ) ) ( hp.1 ω );
  -- Combining the inequalities from h_jarzynski_S and h_ineq, we get:
  have h_combined : (∑ ω ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun ω => W ω < ΔF - ξ), p ω) * Real.exp (-α * (ΔF - ξ)) ≤ Real.exp (-α * ΔF) := by
    simpa only [ Finset.sum_mul _ _ _ ] using le_trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum h_ineq ) h_jarzynski_S;
  convert le_div_iff₀ ( Real.exp_pos _ ) |>.2 h_combined using 1
  rw [← Real.exp_sub]
  congr 1
  ring

/-
**No certain violation.** If `ξ ≥ 0` and some outcome `ω₀` has positive probability
and work at least `ΔF` (so it is *not* a violation), then the total violation
probability is strictly below `1`: Landauer's bound can never be violated with
certainty.
-/
theorem second_law_no_violation_below (p : Ω → ℝ) (hp : IsPMF p) (W : Ω → ℝ)
    (ΔF : ℝ) {ξ : ℝ} (hξ : 0 ≤ ξ) {ω₀ : Ω} (hpω₀ : 0 < p ω₀) (hWω₀ : ΔF ≤ W ω₀) :
    ∑ ω ∈ univ.filter (fun ω => W ω < ΔF - ξ), p ω < 1 := by
  refine' lt_of_le_of_lt ( Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg ( show ( Finset.univ.filter fun ω => W ω < ΔF - ξ ) ⊆ Finset.univ.erase ω₀ from fun ω hω => _ ) fun _ _ _ => hp.1 _ ) _;
  · grind;
  · rw [ ← hp.2, ← Finset.sum_erase_add _ _ ( Finset.mem_univ ω₀ ), add_comm ] ; linarith

/-- **Landauer second-law violation bound.** For one-bit erasure at temperature `T`
and Boltzmann constant `k`, with inverse temperature `α = (kT)⁻¹` and free-energy cost
`ΔF = k·T·log 2`, the probability that the erasure work falls below `k·T·log 2` by a
margin `ξ` is at most `exp(-ξ / (kT))`. -/
theorem landauer_violation_bound (p : Ω → ℝ) (hp : IsPMF p) (W : Ω → ℝ)
    (k T : ℝ) (hk : 0 < k) (hT : 0 < T)
    (hJ : JarzynskiCondition p W (k * T)⁻¹ (k * T * Real.log 2)) (ξ : ℝ) :
    ∑ ω ∈ univ.filter (fun ω => W ω < k * T * Real.log 2 - ξ), p ω
      ≤ Real.exp (-(k * T)⁻¹ * ξ) :=
  second_law_violation_bound p hp W (k * T)⁻¹ (k * T * Real.log 2)
    (inv_pos.2 (mul_pos hk hT)) hJ ξ

/-
**Monotone exponential decay of the violation bound.** As the violation margin `ξ`
increases, the Landauer violation-probability bound `exp(-ξ/(kT))` strictly decreases:
larger violations of Landauer's bound are exponentially rarer.
-/
theorem landauer_violation_decays (k T : ℝ) (hk : 0 < k) (hT : 0 < T)
    {ξ₁ ξ₂ : ℝ} (h : ξ₁ < ξ₂) :
    Real.exp (-(k * T)⁻¹ * ξ₂) < Real.exp (-(k * T)⁻¹ * ξ₁) := by
  exact Real.exp_lt_exp.mpr ( by nlinarith [ inv_pos.mpr ( mul_pos hk hT ) ] )

end LandauerFluctuationBound

end

# Computational Evidence — Landauer's Principle at the Nanoscale (v19a)

This cycle extends the existing Landauer development
(`Logic.JarzynskiLandauer`, `Physics.LandauerSecondLaw`,
`Physics.LandauerSaturation`, `Physics.LandauerRelativeEntropy`,
`Physics.LandauerThermodynamicLimit`) with two new finite-size results.

## 1. Exponential bound on second-law violations (Jarzynski / Chernoff)

**Claim.** With the finite Jarzynski equality `E[exp(-αW)] = exp(-αΔF)` and `α > 0`,
the total probability that the dissipated work falls *below* the free-energy bound by
a margin `ξ` is at most `exp(-α ξ)`:

    P(W < ΔF - ξ) ≤ exp(-α ξ).

**Two-outcome small case.** Take a single bit with `p = (1/2, 1/2)` and work values
`W = (w₀, w₁)`. The Jarzynski equality fixes

    ΔF = -(1/α) · log( (e^{-αw₀} + e^{-αw₁}) / 2 ).

For `α = 1`, `w₀ = 0`, `w₁ = 2`:
* `ΔF = -log((1 + e^{-2})/2) ≈ 0.566`.
* The only outcome with `W < ΔF - ξ` for `ξ = 0.3` is `ω₀` (`W = 0 < 0.266`),
  contributing probability `1/2 = 0.5`.
* Bound: `exp(-1·0.3) ≈ 0.741`.  Indeed `0.5 ≤ 0.741`. ✓

For `ξ = 0.6` the threshold `ΔF - ξ ≈ -0.034 < 0`, so no outcome qualifies, the
left side is `0`, and `0 ≤ exp(-0.6) ≈ 0.549`. ✓

The bound is the finite-size, fluctuation-theorem refinement of the statement
"erasure costs at least `kT log 2`": violations of the bound are not impossible, but
they are *exponentially rare* in the margin `ξ` (measured in units of `1/α = kT`).

## 2. Maximum-entropy / "uniform is worst case" bound

**Claim.** For any initial PMF `p` on a finite memory with `N` states,

    H(p) = log N − D(p ‖ uniform)   and hence   H(p) ≤ log N,

so the Landauer erasure cost `kT·H(p)` is maximised by the uniform distribution.

**Small cases.**
* `N = 2`, `p = (1/2,1/2)`: `H = log 2 ≈ 0.693 = log N`. Saturates. ✓
* `N = 2`, `p = (1, 0)` (already erased): `H = 0 ≤ log 2`. ✓
* `N = 4`, `p = (1/2,1/4,1/8,1/8)`: `H = 1.75·log 2 ≈ 1.213 ≤ log 4 ≈ 1.386`. ✓

The identity is the Gibbs-inequality identity `H(p) = log N − D(p‖u)`; nonnegativity of
`D` (proved in the catalog as `LandauerRelativeEntropy.relativeEntropy_nonneg`) gives
the max-entropy bound directly, so the uniform/`n`-bit cost analysed in
`LandauerThermodynamicLimit` is the most expensive erasure of an `N`-state memory.

Both claims are standard textbook facts; the numerics above are confirmatory sanity
checks. The formal proofs are in `Physics/LandauerFluctuationBound.lean` and
`Physics/LandauerMaxEntropy.lean`.

This cycle added two finite-size results to the catalog's Landauer development
(`Logic.JarzynskiLandauer`, `Physics.LandauerSecondLaw`,
`Physics.LandauerSaturation`, `Physics.LandauerRelativeEntropy`,
`Physics.LandauerThermodynamicLimit`):

  `relativeEntropy_nonneg`), the bound `H(p) ≤ log N`, the generalised Landauer
  bound `kT·H(p) ≤ E[W]` for an *arbitrary* initial distribution, and the

Both categories declared on the v19a menu are the **cross-domain bridge** category:
probability/Chernoff ↔ thermodynamics, and information theory/max-entropy ↔
thermodynamics. The topic ("Landauer's principle") is intrinsically a bridge
between logical/information-theoretic irreversibility and thermodynamic
dissipation, so every result here is framed as such a bridge.

## Conjectures derived from this cycle

### 1. Two-sided concentration of erasure work (Gaussian-tail refinement)
**Conjecture.** If the centred erasure work is bounded, `|W ω − E[W]| ≤ M` on the
support, then in addition to `P(W < ΔF − ξ) ≤ exp(−αξ)` there is a matching
*sub-Gaussian* upper tail, giving `P(|W − E[W]| ≥ t) ≤ 2·exp(−t²/(2M²))`, so the
dissipated work concentrates in an `O(M)` window around its mean.
*The key insight is...* the same moment-generating-function identity that yields the
one-sided Chernoff bound (`second_law_violation_bound`) becomes a Hoeffding-type
two-sided bound once the work range is bounded, because `exp` is then squeezed
between its tangent and a quadratic on `[−M, M]`.
*Why now?* `second_law_violation_bound` already packages `E[exp(−αW)] = exp(−αΔF)`
as a tail bound; adding a bounded-range hypothesis is a small, self-contained step
that upgrades a one-sided to a two-sided nanoscale concentration statement.

### 2. Quadratic finite-size correction via the work variance
**Conjecture.** For bounded centred work there is a strictly positive constant `c(M)`
with `E[W] − ΔF ≥ c(M)·α·Var_p(W)`, i.e. the Jarzynski correction is bounded below
by the work variance, sharpening the qualitative `LandauerSaturation` result
(correction `> 0` iff fluctuating) into a quantitative lower bound.
*The key insight is...* on a bounded range `exp(y) ≥ 1 + y + c·y²`, so the Jensen gap
`log E[exp(−α(W−μ))] ≥ 0` proved in `LandauerSecondLaw` can be replaced by a
quadratic lower bound controlled by the second moment.
*Why now?* `LandauerSaturation` pinned the equality case (`correction = 0 ⇔ no
fluctuations); the natural next quantitative question — *how much* extra work per unit
variance — is exactly this conjecture and reuses the same `add_one_le_exp` machinery.

### 3. Strict maximum-entropy / uniqueness of the worst-case memory
**Conjecture.** Equality `H(p) = log N` holds iff `p` is the uniform distribution, so
the uniform memory is the *unique* most-expensive `N`-state memory to erase.
*The key insight is...* `H(p) = log N − D(p‖uniform)` (proved this cycle as
`shannonEntropy_eq_log_card_sub_relEntropy`) reduces the uniqueness question to the
equality case of Gibbs' inequality `D(p‖q) = 0 ⇔ p = q`, which follows from strict
convexity of `x ↦ x log x` / strictness of `log x < x − 1` for `x ≠ 1`.
*Why now?* The catalog already has the non-strict Gibbs inequality
(`relativeEntropy_nonneg`) and the strict exponential bound
(`LandauerSaturation.expect_add_one_lt_expect_exp`); assembling them into the strict
Gibbs equality case is the missing companion to the max-entropy bound added here.

### 4. Subadditivity of the Landauer cost of composite memories
**Conjecture.** For a product memory with independent components `p = p₁ ⊗ p₂`, the
erasure entropy is additive, `H(p) = H(p₁) + H(p₂)`, and for *correlated* components it
is subadditive, `H(p) ≤ H(p₁) + H(p₂)`, so correlations *reduce* the Landauer cost —
correlated bits are cheaper to erase than independent ones.
*The key insight is...* additivity is the `log` of a product distribution and
subadditivity is again a relative-entropy (mutual-information `I(1;2) ≥ 0`) statement,
so it reuses exactly the Gibbs nonnegativity backbone of this cycle.
*Why now?* `LandauerThermodynamicLimit` proved extensivity `n·kT·log 2` only for the
*independent uniform* register; the correlated case is the physically interesting
generalisation and is one Gibbs application away.

### 5. Pinsker bridge: a distance lower bound on dissipated work
**Conjecture.** The dissipated work controls how far the prepared state is from
equilibrium: `E[W] − ΔF ≥ 2kT·TV(p, q)²`, where `TV` is total-variation distance.
*The key insight is...* combining the relative-entropy formulation of the Landauer
cost (`LandauerRelativeEntropy`) with Pinsker's inequality `D(p‖q) ≥ 2·TV(p,q)²`
turns the thermodynamic bound into an information-geometric distance bound.
*Why now?* The catalog already expresses Landauer's cost as `kT·D(p‖q)`; the only
missing analytic ingredient is Pinsker's inequality, a standard but currently-absent
lemma that would bridge thermodynamics to statistical distance.

# Excluded minors for bias graphs gainable over cyclic groups `ZMod p`

This file develops, from first principles, a small but genuine slice of the theory of
*gain graphs* and *biased graphs* (Zaslavsky, **Zas81**; Gerards; Funk, **Funk15**) and
proves a clean **excluded-minor / realizability** result for gainability over the cyclic
groups `ZMod p`.

## Background

A *gain graph* over a group `G` is a graph in which every oriented edge carries a label
("gain") in `G`, the reverse orientation carrying the inverse label. A cycle is *balanced*
when the product of the gains along it is the identity. The balanced cycles of a gain graph
always form a *linear class* (they satisfy the **theta property**), so every gain graph is a
*biased graph*. The converse fails: not every biased graph arises from a gain function over a
prescribed group `G`; the biased graphs that do are said to be **gainable over `G`** (or
`G`-realizable). Characterizing `G`-gainability by *excluded minors* is a central theme of the
area, directly generalizing matroid representability over `GF(q)`.

## What is formalized here

We work additively, with `G` an `AddCommGroup` (cyclic groups `ZMod p` are the target).

* `theta_sum`, `theta_property` — the abelian theta identity: the three cycles of a theta
  graph have gains `a - b`, `b - c`, `a - c`, and `(a-b)+(b-c) = a-c`. Hence balanced cycles
  satisfy the bias axiom: if two of the three theta cycles are balanced, so is the third.
  This is the foundational fact that *every gain graph is a biased graph*.
* `pathGain`, `switch`, `pathGain_switch`, `closedWalk_gain_switch_invariant` — *switching*
  (gauge transformation by a vertex potential `φ`) changes the gain of a walk only by the
  telescoping term `φ(start) - φ(end)`, hence leaves the gain of every **closed** walk
  invariant. Balance is therefore a switching invariant.
* `Gainable` — a *parallel-class* (digon-bouquet) biased graph is encoded by its balance
  relation `B` on the edge set `Fin n`; it is gainable over `G` iff there is `g : Fin n → G`
  with `B i j ↔ g i = g j`.
* `gainable_setoid_iff_embedding` — when `B` is an equivalence relation (which the theta
  property forces for parallel edges), gainability over `G` is equivalent to the existence of
  an injection from the set of balanced classes `Quotient s` into `G`.
* `gainable_discrete_iff_card`, `gainable_discrete_zmod` — for the *contra-balanced* bouquet
  (all edges pairwise unbalanced) gainability over a finite `G` holds iff `n ≤ |G|`; over
  `ZMod p` iff `n ≤ p`.
* **Excluded minor.** `excludedMinor_not_gainable`: the `(p+1)`-edge contra-balanced bouquet
  is *not* gainable over `ZMod p`, while `excludedMinor_deletion_gainable`: deleting any one
  edge yields the `p`-edge bouquet, which *is* gainable over `ZMod p`. Thus the `(p+1)`-edge
  contra-balanced bouquet is a minor-minimal obstruction (an excluded minor) to
  `ZMod p`-gainability. `gainable_iff_le_card`/`excludedMinor_gainable_zmod_iff` package the

parallel edges between two vertices. For such a bouquet the balance relation must, by the
theta property, be an equivalence relation on the edges, and a gain assignment is exactly a
function on the edges whose kernel partition is that relation. Gainability over `G` should

namespace BiasGraphZp

/-! ## Gain-graph foundations: the theta property -/

section Theta
variable {G : Type*} [AddCommGroup G]

/-
The abelian **theta identity**: the three cycles of a theta graph, whose path-gains are
`a`, `b`, `c`, have cycle-gains `a - b`, `b - c`, `a - c`, and these telescope.
-/
theorem theta_sum (a b c : G) : (a - b) + (b - c) = a - c := by
  module

/-
**Theta property / bias axiom (abelian case).** If two of the three theta cycles are
balanced (cycle-gain `0`), then so is the third. This is the foundational fact that every
gain graph over an abelian group is a biased graph.
-/
theorem theta_property (a b c : G) (h1 : a - b = 0) (h2 : b - c = 0) : a - c = 0 := by
  grind

/-
Symmetric form of the theta property: balance of the first and third cycles forces
balance of the second.
-/
theorem theta_property' (a b c : G) (h1 : a - b = 0) (h3 : a - c = 0) : b - c = 0 := by
  grind

end Theta

/-! ## Switching (gauge transformations) and balance invariance -/

section Switching
variable {G : Type*} [AddCommGroup G] {V : Type*} [Inhabited V]

/-- The gain of a walk along the vertex list `vs`, i.e. the sum of the edge gains
`g vᵢ vᵢ₊₁` over consecutive vertices. -/
def pathGain (g : V → V → G) : List V → G
  | [] => 0
  | [_] => 0
  | u :: v :: rest => g u v + pathGain g (v :: rest)

/-- *Switching* by a vertex potential `φ`: the new gain on the oriented edge `u → v` is
`g u v + φ u - φ v`. -/
def switch (φ : V → G) (g : V → V → G) : V → V → G := fun u v => g u v + φ u - φ v

@[simp] theorem pathGain_nil (g : V → V → G) : pathGain g ([] : List V) = 0 := rfl
@[simp] theorem pathGain_singleton (g : V → V → G) (v : V) : pathGain g [v] = 0 := rfl
theorem pathGain_cons_cons (g : V → V → G) (u v : V) (rest : List V) :
    pathGain g (u :: v :: rest) = g u v + pathGain g (v :: rest) := rfl

/-
**Switching law for walks.** Switching by `φ` changes the gain of the walk `vs` only by
the telescoping boundary term `φ(start) - φ(end)` (with `headI`/`getLastI` the first/last
vertices).
-/
theorem pathGain_switch (φ : V → G) (g : V → V → G) (vs : List V) :
    pathGain (switch φ g) vs = pathGain g vs + φ vs.headI - φ vs.getLastI := by
      induction' n : vs.length using Nat.strong_induction_on with n ih generalizing vs;
      rcases vs with ( _ | ⟨ u, _ | ⟨ v, vs ⟩ ⟩ ) <;> simp_all +decide [ pathGain ];
      · simp +decide [ List.getLastI ];
      · simp +decide [ List.getLastI ];
      · convert congr_arg ( fun x : G => switch φ g u v + x ) ( ih ( List.length ( v :: vs ) ) ( by simpa [ n.symm ] ) ( v :: vs ) rfl ) using 1 ; simp +decide [ switch ] ; abel_nf;
        grind +suggestions

/-
**Balance is a switching invariant.** Along any *closed* walk (`start = end`) switching
leaves the gain unchanged; in particular it preserves balance.
-/
theorem closedWalk_gain_switch_invariant (φ : V → G) (g : V → V → G) (vs : List V)
    (hclosed : vs.headI = vs.getLastI) :
    pathGain (switch φ g) vs = pathGain g vs := by
      rw [ pathGain_switch ];
      rw [ hclosed, add_sub_cancel_right ]

end Switching

/-! ## Gainability of parallel-class (bouquet) biased graphs -/

/-- A bouquet of `n` parallel edges between two vertices, with prescribed **balance relation**
`B` on its edge set `Fin n`, is **gainable over `G`** when there is a gain assignment
`g : Fin n → G` whose two edges form a balanced digon exactly when their gains agree. -/
def Gainable (G : Type*) [AddCommGroup G] (n : ℕ) (B : Fin n → Fin n → Prop) : Prop :=
  ∃ g : Fin n → G, ∀ i j, B i j ↔ g i = g j

section Realizability
variable {G : Type*} [AddCommGroup G] {n : ℕ}

/-
**Reduction to embeddings.** When the balance relation is an equivalence relation `s`
(as the theta property forces for parallel edges), the bouquet is gainable over `G` iff the
set of balanced classes `Quotient s` injects into `G`.
-/
theorem gainable_setoid_iff_embedding (s : Setoid (Fin n)) :
    Gainable G n s.r ↔ Nonempty (Quotient s ↪ G) := by
      constructor;
      · rintro ⟨ g, hg ⟩;
        refine' ⟨ _, _ ⟩;
        exact fun x => Quotient.liftOn' x g fun i j hij => hg i j |>.1 hij;
        intro x y hxy;
        obtain ⟨ i, rfl ⟩ := Quotient.exists_rep x; obtain ⟨ j, rfl ⟩ := Quotient.exists_rep y; simp_all +decide [ Quotient.eq ] ;
      · rintro ⟨ e ⟩;
        refine' ⟨ fun i => e ( Quotient.mk' i ), fun i j => _ ⟩;
        simp +decide [ e.injective.eq_iff ]

/-
**General counting criterion (C1).** When the balance relation is an equivalence relation
`s` and `G` is finite, the bouquet is gainable over `G` iff the number of balanced classes
(`Fintype.card (Quotient s)`) is at most `|G|`. This generalizes the contra-balanced
threshold below from the discrete relation to every equivalence relation.
-/
theorem gainable_setoid_iff_card [Fintype G] (s : Setoid (Fin n)) [DecidableRel s.r] :
    Gainable G n s.r ↔ Fintype.card (Quotient s) ≤ Fintype.card G := by
  rw [gainable_setoid_iff_embedding, Function.Embedding.nonempty_iff_card_le]

/-
**Contra-balanced (discrete) bouquet, embedding form.** When all edges are pairwise
unbalanced, gainability over `G` is exactly the existence of an injection `Fin n ↪ G`.
-/
theorem gainable_discrete_iff_embedding :
    Gainable G n (· = ·) ↔ Nonempty (Fin n ↪ G) := by
      constructor;
      · rintro ⟨ g, hg ⟩;
        exact ⟨ ⟨ g, fun i j hij => hg i j |>.2 hij ⟩ ⟩;
      · rintro ⟨ e ⟩;
        exact ⟨ e, fun i j => by simp +decide [ e.injective.eq_iff ] ⟩

/-
**Contra-balanced bouquet, cardinality form.** Over a finite group `G`, the `n`-edge
contra-balanced bouquet is gainable iff `n ≤ |G|`.
-/
theorem gainable_discrete_iff_card [Fintype G] :
    Gainable G n (· = ·) ↔ n ≤ Fintype.card G := by
      convert gainable_discrete_iff_embedding using 1;
      by_cases h : n ≤ Fintype.card G <;> simp_all +decide [ Fintype.card_subtype ];
      · exact ⟨ fun x => Fintype.equivFin G |>.symm ⟨ x, by linarith [ Fin.is_lt x ] ⟩, fun x y hxy => by simpa [ Fin.ext_iff ] using hxy ⟩;
      · exact iff_of_false ( not_le_of_gt h ) ( by rintro ⟨ f ⟩ ; exact absurd ( Fintype.card_le_of_injective f f.injective ) ( by simpa ) )

end Realizability

/-! ## Excluded minors over `ZMod p` -/

section ZMod
variable {p n : ℕ}

/-
Over the cyclic group `ZMod p` (with `p ≠ 0`), the `n`-edge contra-balanced bouquet is
gainable iff `n ≤ p`.
-/
theorem gainable_discrete_zmod [NeZero p] :
    Gainable (ZMod p) n (· = ·) ↔ n ≤ p := by
      convert gainable_discrete_iff_card ( G := ZMod p ) using 1;
      norm_num [ ZMod.card ]

/-
**Threshold over a prime `p`.**
-/
theorem excludedMinor_gainable_zmod_iff [Fact p.Prime] :
    Gainable (ZMod p) n (· = ·) ↔ n ≤ p := by
      convert gainable_discrete_zmod;
      exact ⟨ Nat.Prime.ne_zero Fact.out ⟩

/-
**The excluded minor.** The `(p+1)`-edge contra-balanced bouquet is *not* gainable over
`ZMod p`: there are not enough gain values to keep `p+1` edges pairwise unbalanced.
-/
theorem excludedMinor_not_gainable [Fact p.Prime] :
    ¬ Gainable (ZMod p) (p + 1) (· = ·) := by
      rw [ excludedMinor_gainable_zmod_iff ] ; norm_num

/-
**Minor-minimality.** Deleting any one edge from the `(p+1)`-edge contra-balanced bouquet
leaves the `p`-edge contra-balanced bouquet, which *is* gainable over `ZMod p`. Hence the
`(p+1)`-edge bouquet is an excluded minor for `ZMod p`-gainability.
-/
theorem excludedMinor_deletion_gainable [Fact p.Prime] :
    Gainable (ZMod p) p (· = ·) := by
      convert gainable_discrete_zmod;
      rotate_left;
      exacts [ p, p, ⟨ Nat.Prime.ne_zero Fact.out ⟩, by simp +decide [ gainable_discrete_zmod ] ]

/-
The same bouquet *is* gainable over the larger cyclic group `ZMod (p+1)`, confirming the
obstruction is specific to the modulus `p`.
-/
theorem excludedMinor_gainable_over_succ [NeZero (p + 1)] :
    Gainable (ZMod (p + 1)) (p + 1) (· = ·) := by
      convert gainable_discrete_zmod;
      rotate_left;
      exacts [ p + 1, p + 1, by infer_instance, by simp +decide [ gainable_discrete_iff_card ] ]

end ZMod

end BiasGraphZp

# The Linear Brown–Erdős–Sós framework

This file develops the combinatorial groundwork surrounding the **(Linear) Brown–Erdős–Sós (BES)
conjecture**.  Recall that for `r`-uniform hypergraphs the BES extremal function `f_r(n; v, e)`
counts the maximum number of edges of an `r`-uniform hypergraph on `n` vertices that contains *no*
`e` edges spanning at most `v` vertices.  The conjecture of Brown, Erdős and Sós (1973) concerns the
critical span value

> `v = (r-2)·e + 3`,

and asserts that on this threshold the extremal function is sub-quadratic, `f_r(n; (r-2)e+3, e) =
o(n²)`.  The single solved instance `r = 3, e = 3`, where the threshold reads `(3-2)·3+3 = 6`, is
exactly the **Ruzsa–Szemerédi `(6,3)`-theorem**: three triples spanning at most six vertices form a
"linear triangle", and forbidding them caps the edge count at `o(n²)`.

The *linear* refinement studies the same threshold under the structural hypothesis of linearity
(any two edges meet in at most one vertex), the regime of Keevash–Long.  This file isolates the
exact, finitary facts that underpin the programme.

## Main results
* `linear_packing_bound` — the **pair-packing / Fisher-type bound**
  `|E(H)| · C(r,2) ≤ C(n,2)` for any linear `r`-uniform hypergraph.
* `linear_span_ge` — the **span lower bound** from incidence double counting: any `k` edges of a
  linear `r`-uniform hypergraph span at least `k·r − C(k,2)` vertices, stated subtraction-free as
  `k·r ≤ |span| + C(k,2)`.
* `total_span_lower_bound` — if every `k` edges span more than `(r-2)k+3` vertices, the *total* span
  exceeds `(r-2)k+3` as well.
* `besThreshold`, `ruzsaSzemeredi_threshold`, `linear_threshold_tight`,
  `linear_threshold_gap`, `linear_meets_threshold` — the **threshold comparison** results: the
  linear span bound matches the BES threshold exactly for `k ∈ {2,3}` (in particular at the
  Ruzsa–Szemerédi point `r=3, k=3`, value `6`), and falls strictly short for `k ≥ 4`, which is
  precisely where the conjecture becomes non-trivial.
* `LinearBESConjecture` — the **open conjecture** itself, stated as an explicit `Prop` (left
  unproven, as it is a major open problem).

open Finset

namespace LinearHypergraph

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-- A finite family of edges is **`r`-uniform** if every edge has exactly `r` vertices. -/
def IsUniform (edges : Finset (Finset V)) (r : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ e ∈ edges, e.card = r

/-- A finite family of edges is **linear** if any two distinct edges meet in at most one vertex. -/
def IsLinear (edges : Finset (Finset V)) : Prop :=
  ∀ e₁ ∈ edges, ∀ e₂ ∈ edges, e₁ ≠ e₂ → (e₁ ∩ e₂).card ≤ 1

/-- The set of vertices **spanned** by a family of edges: the union of all its edges. -/
def span (edges : Finset (Finset V)) : Finset V := edges.biUnion id

omit [Fintype V] in
@[simp] theorem mem_span {edges : Finset (Finset V)} {v : V} :
    v ∈ span edges ↔ ∃ e ∈ edges, v ∈ e := by
  simp [span]

/-! ### Pair-disjointness, the engine of the packing bound -/

omit [Fintype V] in
/-- For a linear family, the "pair sets" `powersetCard 2 e` are pairwise disjoint: a common
2-subset would force two edges to share two vertices. -/
theorem pairs_disjoint {edges : Finset (Finset V)} (hlin : IsLinear edges) :
    (edges : Set (Finset V)).PairwiseDisjoint (fun e => powersetCard 2 e) := by
  intro e he f hf hne
  by_contra h_inter
  have h_card : (e ∩ f).card ≥ 2 := by
    obtain ⟨p, hp₁, hp₂⟩ := Finset.not_disjoint_iff.mp h_inter
    exact Finset.card_le_card (Finset.subset_inter (Finset.mem_powersetCard.mp hp₁ |>.1)
      (Finset.mem_powersetCard.mp hp₂ |>.1)) |> le_trans (Finset.mem_powersetCard.mp hp₁ |>.2.ge)
  linarith [hlin e he f hf hne]

/-- The disjoint union of the per-edge pair sets is contained in the set of all vertex pairs. -/
theorem biUnion_pairs_subset (edges : Finset (Finset V)) :
    edges.biUnion (fun e => powersetCard 2 e) ⊆ (univ : Finset V).powersetCard 2 := by
  intro p hp
  simp only [Finset.mem_biUnion, Finset.mem_powersetCard] at hp ⊢
  obtain ⟨e, _, hpe, hpc⟩ := hp
  exact ⟨Finset.subset_univ p, hpc⟩

/-! ### 1. The linear packing bound -/

/--
**Linear packing bound.** For a linear `r`-uniform hypergraph `H` on `n = |V|` vertices,
`|E(H)| · C(r,2) ≤ C(n,2)`.  Each edge accounts for `C(r,2)` pairs of vertices, linearity makes
these pair-sets disjoint, and there are only `C(n,2)` pairs in total.
-/
theorem linear_packing_bound {edges : Finset (Finset V)} {r : ℕ}
    (huni : IsUniform edges r) (hlin : IsLinear edges) :
    edges.card * r.choose 2 ≤ (Fintype.card V).choose 2 := by
  have h_final : ∑ e ∈ edges, (powersetCard 2 e).card = edges.card * r.choose 2 := by
    rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x hx => by rw [Finset.card_powersetCard, huni x hx]]
    simp +decide
  rw [← h_final, ← Finset.card_biUnion (pairs_disjoint hlin)]
  exact le_trans (Finset.card_le_card (biUnion_pairs_subset edges))
    (by simp +decide [Finset.card_univ, Nat.choose_two_right])

/-! ### 2. The span lower bound -/

/-
**Span lower bound (incidence double count).** Any `k` edges of a linear `r`-uniform hypergraph
span at least `k·r − C(k,2)` vertices.  Stated subtraction-free:
`(#edges)·r ≤ |span edges| + C(#edges, 2)`.

Proof idea: count incidences `∑_v deg(v) = (#edges)·r` and pairs through a vertex
`∑_v C(deg v, 2) = ∑_{e≠f} |e ∩ f| ≤ C(#edges, 2)` (linearity), then use `deg v − 1 ≤ C(deg v, 2)`.
-/
theorem linear_span_ge {edges : Finset (Finset V)} {r : ℕ}
    (huni : IsUniform edges r) (hlin : IsLinear edges) :
    edges.card * r ≤ (span edges).card + (edges.card).choose 2 := by
  have h_deg : ∀ v ∈ span edges, (Finset.card (Finset.filter (fun e => v ∈ e) edges)) ≤ 1 + Nat.choose (Finset.card (Finset.filter (fun e => v ∈ e) edges)) 2 := by
    intro v hv; rcases n : Finset.card ( Finset.filter ( fun e => v ∈ e ) edges ) with ( _ | _ | n ) <;> simp_all +arith +decide [ Nat.choose ] ;
  have h_sum_deg : ∑ v ∈ span edges, Finset.card (Finset.filter (fun e => v ∈ e) edges) = edges.card * r := by
    simp +decide only [card_filter];
    rw [ Finset.sum_comm, Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x hx => ?_ ];
    rw [ Finset.sum_const, smul_eq_mul, mul_comm ];
    simp +decide;
    rw [ Finset.inter_eq_right.mpr ( show x ⊆ span edges from fun v hv => Finset.mem_biUnion.mpr ⟨ x, hx, hv ⟩ ), huni x hx ];
  have h_sum_choose : ∑ v ∈ span edges, Nat.choose (Finset.card (Finset.filter (fun e => v ∈ e) edges)) 2 ≤ Nat.choose edges.card 2 := by
    have h_sum_choose : ∑ v ∈ span edges, Nat.choose (Finset.card (Finset.filter (fun e => v ∈ e) edges)) 2 = ∑ p ∈ Finset.powersetCard 2 edges, (Finset.card (Finset.filter (fun v => ∀ e ∈ p, v ∈ e) (span edges))) := by
      have h_sum_choose : ∀ v ∈ span edges, Nat.choose (Finset.card (Finset.filter (fun e => v ∈ e) edges)) 2 = ∑ p ∈ Finset.powersetCard 2 edges, (if ∀ e ∈ p, v ∈ e then 1 else 0) := by
        intro v hv
        have h_pair_count : Finset.powersetCard 2 (Finset.filter (fun e => v ∈ e) edges) = Finset.filter (fun p => ∀ e ∈ p, v ∈ e) (Finset.powersetCard 2 edges) := by
          grind;
        replace h_pair_count := congr_arg Finset.card h_pair_count; aesop;
      rw [ Finset.sum_congr rfl h_sum_choose, Finset.sum_comm ] ; simp +decide ;
    -- Since each pair of edges intersects in at most one vertex, the number of vertices in the intersection of any two edges is at most 1.
    have h_inter : ∀ p ∈ Finset.powersetCard 2 edges, (Finset.card (Finset.filter (fun v => ∀ e ∈ p, v ∈ e) (span edges))) ≤ 1 := by
      intro p hp; rw [ Finset.mem_powersetCard ] at hp; obtain ⟨ e₁, e₂, he₁, he₂, he ⟩ := Finset.card_eq_two.mp hp.2; simp_all +decide [ Finset.subset_iff ] ;
      exact le_trans ( Finset.card_le_card ( show Finset.filter ( fun v => v ∈ e₁ ∧ v ∈ e₂ ) ( span edges ) ⊆ e₁ ∩ e₂ from fun x hx => by aesop ) ) ( hlin e₁ hp.1 e₂ hp.2 he₁ );
    exact h_sum_choose.symm ▸ le_trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum h_inter ) ( by simp +decide );
  exact h_sum_deg ▸ le_trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum h_deg ) ( by simp +decide [ Finset.sum_add_distrib ] ; linarith )

omit [Fintype V] in
/--
**Total span lower bound.** If every `k` edges of `H` span more than `(r-2)·k + 3` vertices, then
(provided `H` has at least `k` edges) the *whole* family spans more than `(r-2)·k + 3` vertices:
a `k`-subset witnesses the bound and its span is contained in the total span.
-/
theorem total_span_lower_bound {edges : Finset (Finset V)} {r k : ℕ}
    (hkm : k ≤ edges.card)
    (hspan : ∀ S ⊆ edges, S.card = k → (r - 2) * k + 3 < (span S).card) :
    (r - 2) * k + 3 < (span edges).card := by
  obtain ⟨S, hSsub, hScard⟩ := Finset.exists_subset_card_eq hkm
  have hlt := hspan S hSsub hScard
  have hmono : span S ⊆ span edges :=
    Finset.biUnion_subset_biUnion_of_subset_left id hSsub
  exact lt_of_lt_of_le hlt (Finset.card_le_card hmono)

/-! ### 3. Threshold comparison and the Ruzsa–Szemerédi point -/

/-- The **Brown–Erdős–Sós span threshold** `(r-2)·k + 3` for `k` edges of an `r`-uniform
hypergraph. -/
def besThreshold (r k : ℕ) : ℕ := (r - 2) * k + 3

/-- At the Ruzsa–Szemerédi point `r = 3, k = 3`, the BES threshold equals `6`: forbidding three
triples on at most six vertices is the `(6,3)`-problem. -/
theorem ruzsaSzemeredi_threshold : besThreshold 3 3 = 6 := by
  decide

/--
**Threshold tightness for small `k`.** For `k = 2` and `k = 3` (and `r ≥ 2`) the linear span bound
is exactly tight against the BES threshold:
`k·r = besThreshold r k + C(k,2)`.  Hence linearity *alone* forces any `k ≤ 3` edges to span at
least `besThreshold r k` vertices.
-/
theorem linear_threshold_tight {r k : ℕ} (hr : 2 ≤ r) (hk : k = 2 ∨ k = 3) :
    k * r = besThreshold r k + k.choose 2 := by
  rcases hk with rfl | rfl <;> simp only [besThreshold, Nat.choose] <;> omega

/--
**Threshold gap for `k = 4`.** From `k = 4` on, the linear span bound falls strictly short of the
BES threshold: `besThreshold r 4 + C(4,2) = 4·r + 1 > 4·r`.  This is the first `k` where the linear
span bound no longer guarantees the BES span condition, marking the onset of the open regime.
-/
theorem linear_threshold_gap {r : ℕ} (hr : 2 ≤ r) :
    4 * r < besThreshold r 4 + (4).choose 2 := by
  simp only [besThreshold, Nat.choose]
  omega

/--
**Linearity meets the threshold for `k ≤ 3`.** Combining the span lower bound with threshold
tightness: any `k ∈ {2,3}` edges of a linear `r`-uniform hypergraph (`r ≥ 2`) span at least
`besThreshold r k` vertices.
-/
theorem linear_meets_threshold {edges : Finset (Finset V)} {r k : ℕ}
    (huni : IsUniform edges r) (hlin : IsLinear edges)
    (hr : 2 ≤ r) (hcard : edges.card = k) (hk : k = 2 ∨ k = 3) :
    besThreshold r k ≤ (span edges).card := by
  have h1 := linear_span_ge huni hlin
  rw [hcard] at h1
  have h2 := linear_threshold_tight (r := r) (k := k) hr hk
  omega

/-! ### 4. The open conjecture -/

/--
**The Linear Brown–Erdős–Sós conjecture** (for parameters `r` and `k`).

A linear `r`-uniform hypergraph in which every `k` edges span more than the BES threshold
`(r-2)k+3` vertices has a *sub-quadratic* number of edges: for every `ε > 0` there is `N` such that
for all `n ≥ N`, every such hypergraph on `n` vertices has at most `ε·n²` edges.

This is a major open problem; it is solved only for `r = 3, k = 3` (the Ruzsa–Szemerédi
`(6,3)`-theorem).  It is stated here as an explicit `Prop` and deliberately left **unproven**. -/
def LinearBESConjecture (r k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ (n : ℕ), N ≤ n →
    ∀ (W : Type) [Fintype W] [DecidableEq W], Fintype.card W = n →
      ∀ (edges : Finset (Finset W)),
        IsUniform edges r → IsLinear edges →
        (∀ S ⊆ edges, S.card = k → (r - 2) * k + 3 < (span S).card) →
        (edges.card : ℝ) ≤ ε * (n : ℝ) ^ 2

end LinearHypergraph

# Computational Evidence — Excluded minors for `ZMod p`-gainable bias graphs

All claims below are *also* formalized and machine-checked in
`Catalog/Novelty/BiasGraphsZp.lean` (0 sorries, standard axioms only). This note
records the small-case evidence that guided the formalization.

## 1. Object under study

A **bouquet** `B_n` is `n` parallel edges between two vertices. Its balance
relation is, by the theta property, an equivalence relation on the `n` edges; a
gain assignment over a group `G` is a map `g : Fin n → G` whose kernel partition
realizes that relation. The **contra-balanced** bouquet `U_n` is the one in which
all edges are pairwise unbalanced (the discrete relation `=`), so a realization is
exactly an injection `Fin n ↪ G`.

## 2. Small-case calculations: when is `U_n` gainable over `ZMod p`?

`U_n` gainable over `ZMod p` ⟺ there exist `n` pairwise-distinct values in `ZMod p`
⟺ `n ≤ p`. Number of valid gain assignments = `p · (p-1) ··· (p-n+1)` (falling
factorial), which is positive iff `n ≤ p`:

| p \ n | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|-------|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2     | 2 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 3     | 3 | 6 | 6 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 5     | 5 |20 |60 |120|120| 0 |

The first `0` in row `p` occurs at `n = p+1`: `U_{p+1}` is the smallest
contra-balanced bouquet *not* gainable over `ZMod p`.

## 3. Excluded-minor / minor-minimality check

* `U_{p+1}` is **not** `ZMod p`-gainable (`p+1 > p`).
* Deleting any one edge gives `U_p`, which **is** `ZMod p`-gainable (`p ≤ p`,
  a bijection `Fin p ↔ ZMod p`).
* `U_{p+1}` **is** `ZMod q`-gainable for every `q ≥ p+1` (e.g. `q = p+1`).

Hence `U_{p+1}` is a minor-minimal obstruction (an excluded minor) for
`ZMod p`-gainability — the gain-graph analogue of `U_{2,q+2}` being an excluded
minor for `GF(q)`-representability of matroids.

## 4. OEIS note

The gainability thresholds read off the table are the trivial diagonal `n = p+1`;
the count of realizations is the falling factorial `p^{\underline n}` (A008279).
No new integer sequence is needed; the content is the structural threshold, which
is what we formalize.

## 5. Counterexample hunt

We searched for a contra-balanced bouquet `U_n` gainable over `ZMod p` with `n > p`:
none exists (pigeonhole, formalized as `gainable_discrete_zmod`). We also checked
the abelian theta identity `(a-b)+(b-c)=(a-c)` on random triples in `ZMod 7`,
`ZMod 11`: always holds (formalized as `theta_sum`).

# Future Directions — Excluded minors for bias graphs gainable over `ZMod p`

Built on the verified results in `Catalog/Novelty/BiasGraphsZp.lean`:
the abelian theta property (every gain graph is a biased graph), switching
invariance of balance, the reduction of bouquet gainability to embeddings of the
balanced-class quotient, and the headline excluded minor: the `(p+1)`-edge
contra-balanced bouquet `U_{p+1}` is minor-minimally non-`ZMod p`-gainable, while
gainable over every larger cyclic group. The following conjectures are precise and
falsifiable, ordered roughly by ambition.

## C1. Sharp threshold for arbitrary bouquets (counting form) — **RESOLVED**
For *any* equivalence relation `s` on `Fin n` (a general parallel-class biased
graph, not just the contra-balanced one), the bouquet is `G`-gainable for finite
`G` **iff** the number of `s`-classes is `≤ |G|`. This is now proved as
`gainable_setoid_iff_card` in `Catalog/Novelty/BiasGraphsZp.lean` (combining
`gainable_setoid_iff_embedding` with `Embedding.nonempty_iff_card_le`), with the
contra-balanced threshold `gainable_discrete_zmod` as the `s = ⊥` special case.
*Next step:* package the explicit `ZMod p` corollary
`Gainable (ZMod p) n s.r ↔ Fintype.card (Quotient s) ≤ p` and extend to a
minor-minimality statement for non-discrete balanced classes.

## C2. Gainability over a *general* finite abelian group depends only on the
class count, not the group structure.
For finite abelian `G, H` with `|G| = |H|`, a parallel-class biased graph is
`G`-gainable iff it is `H`-gainable. **Test:** both sides reduce, via
`gainable_setoid_iff_embedding`, to `#classes ≤ |G| = |H|`. Predicts that for
*bouquets* the cyclic restriction `ZMod p` is no weaker than any abelian group of
the same order — i.e. the excluded minors `U_{q+1}` are insensitive to whether the
modulus is prime. (Sharpness/breakdown for *non-bouquet* graphs is the interesting
boundary.)

## C3. The excluded-minor family is exactly `{U_{p+1}}` for parallel-class graphs.
Among parallel-class biased graphs, the *complete* list of excluded minors for
`ZMod p`-gainability is the single graph `U_{p+1}`. **Test:** show every
non-`ZMod p`-gainable parallel-class biased graph contains `U_{p+1}` as a minor
(restriction to `p+1` pairwise-unbalanced edges), using C1. This is the
parallel-class analogue of a finite excluded-minor characterization.

## C4. Rank-2 / two-vertex non-parallel obstructions and the prime gap.
Move beyond bouquets to graphs with two vertices joined by parallel edges *plus*
loops at the vertices (loops carry gains too; a loop is balanced iff its gain is
`0`). Conjecture: introducing `k` distinct nonzero loop gains lowers the bouquet
threshold from `p` to `p - 1` whenever a loop is forced unbalanced, producing a
*new* excluded minor `U'_{p}` distinct from `U_{p+1}`. **Test:** extend `Gainable`
with a loop-gain component and recompute the threshold; falsified if the threshold
stays `p`.

## C5. Switching-reduced normal form and an algorithmic gainability test.
Using `closedWalk_gain_switch_invariant`, conjecture that every `ZMod p`-gain
graph on a connected base graph is switching-equivalent to one supported on a
spanning tree with `0` gains (a "tree-gauge"), so that gainability of a biased
graph reduces to solving a single linear system over `ZMod p` indexed by the
fundamental cycles. **Test:** formalize the tree-gauge existence
(`∃ φ, switch φ g` vanishes on a chosen spanning tree) and derive that the
balanced cycle space is the kernel of the fundamental-cycle gain map; this would
turn `ZMod p`-gainability into a decidable rank condition, generalizing the
counting criterion of C1 to graphs of arbitrary cyclomatic number.
